documentation: Paths in the public mirror targets that the corvidae transform must never write, and the keys it must not author inside the files it does write. Change detection in the mirror works by transforming into a clone of the target and asking git whether anything differs: an empty `git status --porcelain` means skip the sync. That only holds when this enumeration is exhaustive, so a missing entry degrades the mirror into 'always open a pull request'. `paths` is enforced by the guard in `target-owned.ts`, over a plan's writes and, since COR-1221, over its deletions. `retired` is the opposite list and the only place a whole target directory may be removed; it is enforced by the same guard and never relaxes `paths`. `insideFiles` states the ownership default for the structured files the transform does write — manifests and tsconfigs — which a whole-file guard cannot express; it is applied by `manifests.ts` and `typescript-configuration.ts` rather than by the guard. `targets` names the public repositories an entry applies to; omit it when the entry applies to every target.

paths.reason: Root license is repository-facing and target-owned. Evidence: weft ships a root LICENSE, cinder ships none at all, while every published package in both targets declares `"license": "MIT"`. A file whose presence differs between the two targets is not a transform output. Per-package LICENSE is transform-owned and stays writable: weft's `files` arrays list it and the transform fans it out to satisfy them.

Root README describes the public repository, its badges and its install story, and is target-owned. This bare glob matches only the repository root (verified against Bun.Glob: `README.md` does not match `packages/weft/README.md`), which is deliberate rather than an oversight to widen: a package-root `README.md` is target-owned too, by the same default every other unenumerated path gets under COR-1223's inversion, and does not need a second entry here to say so. Every corvidae workspace's own README is internal documentation — `workspace:*` install instructions, references to the corvidae root, to sibling private workspaces, to `bun run validate` — that would overwrite a target's public npm front page if the transform emitted it blindly, which an earlier, reverted change (COR-1196 round 10) did. `@lostgradient/weft`'s is the one exception: `source.ts`'s `additionalSourceRoots['@lostgradient/weft']` declares it by name, the same way a workspace opts any file outside `src/` into the plan, because its README carries no internal reference and was written for npm from the start. A future package that wants the same treatment declares its own entry there; `packaging.ts`'s `checkReadmePublicity` refuses a packed tarball whose README is missing or still reads as internal, which is what actually prevents a declaration (or a future blanket emission) from shipping the wrong page — this entry's job is only to describe the root file, not to police the per-package ones a declaration already gates.

retired.policy: A directory, or since COR-1286 a single file, that a target still carries and the transform is to remove outright, named here and nowhere else. This is the one deletion in the mirror that is not bounded by what the transform emits. COR-1221 ruled that a sync prunes only beneath the prefixes it writes, so a path the plan says nothing about survives; that rule is what keeps a target's working documents, build scripts and unrelated trees safe, and it is deliberately not relaxed. The inferred version of this capability — 'delete anything in the target the plan did not emit' — would delete every one of those, so a retirement is never derived from the plan's silence. Every entry requires all four keys: `directory` (the target-relative directory or file removed, matched as itself and, for a directory, as a prefix too — `target-owned.ts`'s `walkRetiredPath` tells the two apart by `lstat`, so the key needed no schema change to carry a file), `target` (exactly one repository, singular so that an entry can never retire a path from a target nobody considered), `reason` (why the path is retired rather than synced) and `issue` (the Linear identifier whose sync pull request carries the removal, so a reviewer sees the deletion against a ruling). Relationship to `paths`: a retirement never overrides one. `loadTargetOwnedPolicy` refuses a `retired.directory` that a `paths` glob already claims for the same target, and `collectRetiredPaths` refuses a retirement whose contents include a target-owned file, naming both entries. Neither is a precedence rule — both are failures, because 'the target owns this' and 'the transform deletes this' cannot both be true and picking a winner would delete something nobody ruled on. The other half of a retirement is out of band: a directory or file a target's own CI, hooks or documentation reference has to lose those references in the target's own pull request, which the transform cannot write and must not try to.

entries.reason: The monorepo is weft-ui's home. Until COR-1455 folded the UI into `packages/weft` (as `src/ui`), `layout-map.json` routed `@lostgradient/weft-ui` to the cinder target, so the weft sync has never written this directory and weft's copy has drifted away from corvidae's: it hand-writes `TimeRange` as an optional-property object under a comment claiming the two are structurally identical, which `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` falsifies, and a live dry run failed weft's own `ui-typecheck` and `ui-e2e` on it. Nothing external depends on either copy — `@lostgradient/weft-ui` returns 404 on the registry and was never published — so the drifted copy is removed rather than reconciled. Retired rather than deferred because deferring emits nothing and leaves the directory in place, which is the state that produced the failure.

COR-1455 moved the UI out of its own workspace into `packages/weft` (`src/ui`, with its browser tooling and coverage ratchet under `scripts/ui-browser` and `scripts/ui-coverage`), by the Weft UI project's owner ruling (2026-10-13) that the UI is part of `@lostgradient/weft` and has no mirror of its own. Corvidae has no `@lostgradient/weft-ui` workspace any more, so no cinder sync writes this directory again, and the copy the cinder mirror carries is unpublished source (`@lostgradient/weft-ui` returns 404 on the registry) that would stay behind unmaintained beside the Weft mirror's live copy. Retired rather than left in place, because a sync prunes only beneath the prefixes it writes and the plan no longer names this one. Out of band: the directory's one target-owned file, its `CHANGELOG.md`, which `collectRetiredPaths` would refuse to delete, was already removed in the cinder repository's own commit `f46fcf9c` ("Delete the target-owned files left in packages/chat and packages/weft-ui"). The only other file there that names `packages/weft-ui` is the transform-emitted `mirror-verify.yaml`, which the same sync regenerates without it.

COR-1286's ruling: a mirror runs one transform-emitted verification workflow (`mirror-verify.yaml`, whose jobs are exactly `verifyTarget`'s steps) plus the release workflow, unchanged. `ci.yaml` is weft's pull-request CI gate that `mirror-verify.yaml` replaces; every script it runs (`lint`, `typecheck`, `test`, `test:coverage`, `build`, the example workflows) is target-side tooling `verifyTarget` does not exercise, so the file becomes dead CI once the mirror opens its own PR-time workflow. `packages/weft/scripts/ci-workflows.test.ts`, which reads this file directly, is retired in the same pull request so its assertions are never left pointing at a path that no longer exists.

A path-filtered PR-time re-run of documentation and JSDoc checks (`verify:documentation`, `build`, `verify:jsdoc`, `verify:jsdoc:doctests`, `verify:jsdoc:declarations`, `verify:markdown-doctests`) that `packages/weft/scripts/run-gates.ts`'s `validate` and `prepack` pipelines already gate at release time through `release.yaml`. Those package.json scripts and the scripts they call (`verify-documentation.ts`, `audit-jsdoc-manifest.ts`, `verify-jsdoc-doctests.ts`, `check-declaration-jsdoc.ts`, `extract-markdown-doctests.ts`) are called by the release workflow and stay; only this redundant standalone PR-time workflow file is retired.

Git hook scripts. Corvidae's own AGENTS.md forbids Git-hook installation, and COR-1286's ruling removes rather than merely ignores everything the target carries for its own CI that is not the release workflow or a workflow the mirror itself emits. Weft's root `prepare` script (`husky && bun packages/weft/scripts/husky/verify-hooks-installed.ts`) still names this directory after the retirement; per this policy's own 'out of band' clause, removing that reference is the target's own follow-up pull request, not something the transform writes.

The hook-verification helpers `.husky`'s scripts invoke (`verify-hooks-installed.ts`, `pre-commit.ts`, `post-checkout.ts`, `post-merge.ts`, `run-tests.ts`, `utilities.ts` and their tests). Hook infrastructure, not package source; retired alongside `.husky` in the same pull request for the same reason, with the same out-of-band follow-up needed for the root `prepare` script's reference to `verify-hooks-installed.ts`.

Reads `.github/workflows/ci.yaml` and `release.yaml` directly and asserts their Bun pin and install flags. Once `ci.yaml` is retired in this same pull request, `readWorkflow('ci.yaml')` would throw on a file that no longer exists, so this test is retired with its subject rather than left to fail. D3 (COR-1286) is what makes a single file, rather than only a directory, a legal `retired` entry — this is the file that motivated it. Verified this is the only file in the weft seed reading either workflow's path outside fixture-built test data (`verify-documentation.test.ts` builds a synthetic `.github/workflows/ci.yaml` fixture rather than reading the real one, so it is unaffected).

insideFiles.policy: The ownership default inside a manifest or a tsconfig the transform writes, for a file the target ALREADY carries. COR-1223 inverted it. The transform used to emit corvidae's whole manifest and preserve a short enumerated list of exceptions; a live dry run against a seeded copy of the weft repository failed twelve of that repository's twenty checks, because the enumeration was a list of instances of a class it never named. Naming the class: the transform owns the *published surface* — what corvidae's source becomes once it is built and packed — and the target owns *everything that describes a repository corvidae is not*. So for an existing file the target's own copy is the base, the keys below are overlaid onto it, and anything not listed stays exactly as the target had it. A file the target does NOT carry has nothing to preserve, so corvidae's is emitted whole. The two enumerations that used to live here as `fields` pointers — `/scripts/prepare`, `/devDependencies/husky`, `/lint-staged` — are subsumed: none of them is overlaid, so all three survive by default along with every key nobody thought to enumerate. `/version` was a fourth such pointer and is no longer: COR-1196 moved it into `manifestDefaults` below, because 'survives by default' silently meant 'never gets a version at all' for a workspace the target already had a manifest for but no `version` key in it.

manifestKeys.reason: The public name is the mirror's own ruling, recorded in `package-map.json`. A target carrying a different name for the same workspace is a target the map has to be corrected against, not a fact to preserve.
Presence follows the disposition: stripped from anything the map publishes, forced on everything else. A published package that kept a stray `private: true` could never be released.

Root only, and the transform's because `layout-map.json` is what decides where each workspace lands. Preserving the target's globs would leave a workspace the transform emits — `internal/typescript` in the cinder target — outside the graph its own siblings resolve through.

Root only, and the transform's because it is computed rather than copied: corvidae's catalog plus one entry per cross-target edge the plan resolved. Preserving the target's drops those additions while the package manifests that reference them still say `catalog:`, which is a root the staged install cannot resolve. Absent for a target with no workspace root to hold one, where this entry then removes it.

The subpath map IS the published surface, regenerated from corvidae's source by `package-surface.json` and gated against the registry baseline by `checkParity`. Preserving the target's would let a subpath corvidae's source no longer provides keep being advertised.
The publish allowlist is computed alongside `exports` and checked against it by `checkTargetCoverage`; the pair only means anything when both come from the same pass.
Executable entry points are part of what a consumer installs, and `checkTargetCoverage` rules on them against `files` exactly as it does on `exports`.
A bundler's licence to drop unreferenced modules from the built artifact. It is a claim about corvidae's source, which is the source the artifact is built from.

manifestDefaults.reason: Legacy entry point. `package-surface.json` records it, but its own documentation says that record is a port of what the target publishes today — so where the target still carries the key, the target holds the authoritative copy of the same fact.
Registry access and tag are a release decision belonging to whoever publishes, which is the target's release tooling.
The runtime floor a published package advertises is a support commitment the target makes to its consumers; corvidae's floor tracks whatever Bun the workspace happens to run.

COR-1196: `manifests.ts`'s `rewriteWorkspaceManifest` always seeds `emitted.version` (`0.0.0`, or `package-map.json`'s `lastPublishedVersion` for a workspace the target has no manifest for at all), but `version` was never in `manifestKeys` or `manifestDefaults`, so for a workspace the target already has *a* manifest for, `composeManifest` based `{...existing}` and neither loop ever supplied the seed. A private workspace whose existing manifest predates this table having an opinion — `@lostgradient/testing`, whose target manifest carries no `version` at all — was emitted with none, and `bun pm pack` refused every consumer with "Failed to resolve workspace version" in `devDependencies`. `manifestDefaults`' own rule, "supply only where the target has none of its own," is exactly the fix: an existing target version is still untouched, and a workspace with a manifest but no version now gets the same seed a brand-new one always did.

dependencies.policy: Classification is the target's, ranges follow the package that declares them, and nothing is silently dropped. Three cases, applied to the union of corvidae's `dependencies`, `devDependencies` and `optionalDependencies` and the target's. `peerDependencies` is deliberately not one of them: a peer range is half of a packaging declaration whose other half is `peerDependenciesMeta`, so the pair is composed together, by name, under `peerDependencies` below rather than split across these three cases. (1) A package that ships from this mirror is the transform's outright — name, block and specifier — because only the transform knows what it is called downstream and whether the edge stays a `workspace:*`. Its stale entries are removed first, so an edge corvidae dropped does not linger. (2) A third-party package the target declares anywhere keeps the target's block and the target's range. Weft putting `better-sqlite3` in `optionalDependencies` and `peerDependencies` is a packaging decision of weft's; corvidae having it in `dependencies` is an artifact of being an internal workspace where every dependency is a plain one, and emitting that moves seven storage drivers into every consumer's install. (3) A third-party package the target declares nowhere is added in corvidae's own block at corvidae's own range, and reported as `addedDependencies`: a package legitimately gains a dependency, and the alternative to adding it is emitting source that cannot resolve its own imports. The asymmetry with `scripts`, which are never unioned, is deliberate: a dependency is a fact about the source, while a script is a choice about the repository. COR-1287 widened case (1) to the target's own spelling: `mirrorPackages` carries not just each workspace's public name but the name the target's manifest at that workspace's directory already uses, where the two differ. The since-retired agent-bureau target called corvidae's `@lostgradient/lifecycle` just `lifecycle`, and under the public name alone rule (1) never matched that entry while rule (2) kept it, so the composed manifest declared the same workspace twice under two names and `bun install` refused the staged tree. The alias is read off the clone at the directory `layout-map.json` assigns, never recorded, and a target name that collides with a *different* workspace's public name is a hard failure rather than an alias.

peerDependencies.policy: COR-1468. Peer ranges and `peerDependenciesMeta` are one packaging declaration and are composed as a pair, name by name, so the two halves can never drift apart. For each peer a workspace's own corvidae manifest declares in `peerDependencies`, corvidae's range and its `peerDependenciesMeta` entry win over both the target's existing value and the vendored `package-surface.json` entry — including the absence of a meta entry, which declares a required peer and so removes an `optional` entry the other side held for that name. A declared peer is a fact about corvidae's source: Weft's A2A subpath imports `@a2a-js/sdk` and must not install it into every consumer, and a hand edit after the sync to say so is exactly what `publication-history.ts` refuses. Every peer corvidae does not declare keeps today's answer: the target's range and meta where the target has `peerDependencies`, otherwise the vendored `package-surface.json` entry, which is a port of what the target published. A workspace that declares no peers composes exactly as before. `manifests.ts`'s `composeManifest` merges the declarations into a target manifest's pair; `surface.ts`'s `applySurfaceToManifest` handles only a target without `peerDependencies`, merging the declarations over the vendored entry, and passes an already-composed pair through unchanged.

insideFiles.typeScriptTargetOwnedPolicy: The keys below are read back out of the target's own `tsconfig*.json`; everything else in the emitted file comes from the transform. That is one key in practice, `extends`, and it is not enumerated because it is not a choice the transform makes per target: `@lostgradient/typescript` is what corvidae's source is written against — `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` alone is why hundreds of weft files differ from upstream's — so the compiler options always come from the shared configuration, vendored where the target cannot hold the package. Enumerating it would be a list nothing reads.

typeScriptTargetOwned.reason: Which trees a repository type-checks is that repository's decision about its own working directories. Weft's `include` is `src` plus five named `scripts/*.ts` files; corvidae's is `src`, `tests`, `scripts`, `examples`. Emitting corvidae's widened it over the target's `examples/`, which import the package by its public name and resolve through `exports` to a `dist/` that does not exist when `typecheck` runs, and over the target's own `scripts/`, which it had deliberately never checked.
The other half of `include`; the two only mean anything together.

exceptions.policy: A temporary exception holds an additional path as target-owned for the duration of a transition, then disappears. Every entry requires all four keys: `glob` (the path held), `reason` (what transition requires it), `issue` (the Linear identifier that removes it) and `expires` (an ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` date). The guard fails when `expires` is on or before the current date, so an exception cannot rot silently — a reviewer must either move the date forward, which is a fresh review, or delete the entry. An exception without an expiry date is not reviewable and an expiry date without an issue is not actionable, so both are mandatory. Entries here are additive: they never relax a `paths` entry.

openQuestions: Root tooling configuration — `turbo.json`, `bunfig.toml`, root `tsconfig*.json`, `.oxlintrc.json`, `.prettierrc.json`, `.prettierignore`, `.stylelintrc.json`, `.editorconfig`, `.env.example` — is unresolved. Cinder carries four root tsconfigs where corvidae has one plus `internal/typescript`, so whether the transform generates these or the target owns them depends on the layout mapping, which is a different issue. Resolve before the first real sync run; leaving them out of `paths` is not a ruling that they are transform-owned. COR-1223 settled only the per-workspace `tsconfig*.json` the transform already writes, and only partly: `insideFiles.typeScriptTargetOwned` gives the target its `include` and `exclude`, while everything else in the emitted file comes from the shared configuration. What that discards is the rest of the target's own `compilerOptions`, which weft inlines rather than extending — `paths`, `rootDir`, `typeRoots`, `incremental`, `tsBuildInfoFile`, `assumeChangesOnlyAffectDirectDependencies`, `diagnostics`. None of them is load-bearing today (`@/*` is imported by nothing in either checkout, and the rest are caching and reporting), but the ruling is 'the shared configuration wins', not 'the target had nothing worth keeping'; a target that adds a compiler option corvidae's configuration cannot express reopens this.

One-off target working documents (cinder's `AB-429-final-contract-review.md` is the current example) cannot be enumerated ahead of time. COR-1221 settled what that means: the transform now deletes, but only beneath the paths it owns, which are the source trees it emits, plus the directories `retired` names — the one exception, and the reason it is an enumeration rather than an inference. A path outside both — a working document, a build script, anything nobody enumerated — is never deleted, so this class never needed enumerating. The enumeration itself is no longer write-only either: `assertDeletablePaths` runs the same list over a plan's deletions, so a target-owned path inside a source tree is refused as a delete exactly as it is refused as a write.
